entries.title: Replacement cost vs. actual cash value
entries.caption:
Two policies can cover the same couch and pay very different amounts. The difference often comes down to two phrases. 🛋️

REPLACEMENT COST coverage is designed to pay what it costs to replace a damaged item with a new one of similar kind and quality. ACTUAL CASH VALUE pays what the item was worth at the time of the loss, which means depreciation for age and wear is subtracted. On older belongings, that gap can be big.

Many home policies handle the house itself and your personal belongings differently, so it's worth checking both. Some policies also pay actual cash value first and the rest once the item is actually replaced.

Not sure which one your policy uses? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com for a free coverage review.

Coverage varies by policy, state and eligibility.

entries.title: Renting? Your landlord's policy isn't yours
entries.caption:
One of the most common renter surprises: "I figured the landlord's insurance would cover it." 🏢

Your landlord's policy is generally built to protect the building and the landlord's own liability, not your personal belongings. If a fire, burst pipe or break-in damages your furniture, electronics or clothes, that's typically where renters insurance comes in.

Many renters policies also include personal liability, which can help if someone is hurt in your unit or you accidentally damage someone else's property, and additional living expenses if a covered loss forces you to stay somewhere else for a while.

Renting and not sure what you'd be covered for? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com and we'll walk through it.

Coverage varies by policy, state and eligibility.

entries.title: What if the other driver has no insurance?
entries.caption:
You can drive carefully and still get hit by someone with little or no insurance. That's exactly the gap uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage is designed for. 🚗

UNINSURED motorist coverage can help pay for your injuries, and in some cases damage to your car, when the at-fault driver has no insurance or it's a hit-and-run. UNDERINSURED motorist coverage can help when the at-fault driver has insurance, but not enough to cover your costs.

What's included, and whether it covers injuries, vehicle damage or both, depends on your policy and your state.

Want to know if you have it and how much? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com for a quick review.

entries.title: Make a home inventory before you need one
entries.caption:
If you had to list everything in your home after a fire or break-in, how much would you forget? Most people forget a lot. 📱

A home inventory makes a claim faster and less stressful, and it helps you see whether your personal property limit is high enough. The easy version takes about 20 minutes:
• Record a slow video walking through every room
• Open closets, cabinets and drawers, and don't skip the garage
• Talk through bigger items as you go (brand, roughly when you bought it)
• Snap photos of receipts or serial numbers for electronics and jewelry
• Save it to cloud storage or email it to yourself so it survives if your home doesn't

entries.title: How much life insurance is enough?
entries.caption:
"How much life insurance do I need?" There's no one-size answer, but there is a simple way to start thinking about it. 💡

Many people begin by adding up what their family would need if their income stopped:
• Debts that would still need paying, including the mortgage
• Years of income your family would need replaced
• Future goals, like college for the kids
• Final expenses
Then subtract savings and any coverage you already have, like a policy through work.

It's a starting point, not a formula. Your real number depends on your goals, your budget and the people who rely on you. This post is educational only. Want to talk it through? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com.

entries.title: Lending your car? Your insurance goes with it
entries.caption:
A friend asks to borrow your car for the weekend. Before you hand over the keys, it helps to know whose insurance is on the hook. 🔑

In many cases, auto insurance follows the car, not the driver. That means if someone you let borrow your car causes an accident, your policy is often the first to respond, and the claim can show up on your insurance history.

Policies handle this differently. Some limit or exclude coverage for drivers who live with you but aren't listed, or for regular use of your car. The other driver's own insurance may help after your limits are used up.

entries.caption:
Holiday hosting season is here. If a guest slips on your icy front steps, do you know how your home policy would respond? 🏠

Most homeowners and renters policies include PERSONAL LIABILITY coverage. If you're found responsible for a guest's injury, it can help pay for their medical bills and your legal defense, up to your policy's limit. Many policies also include MEDICAL PAYMENTS coverage, which can help with a guest's smaller medical bills regardless of who was at fault.

A few easy ways to keep guests safe:
• Clear and de-ice steps, walkways and the driveway
• Light up entryways and stairs
• Keep pets secured when the door is opening a lot

entries.title: Frozen pipes: is the water damage covered?
entries.caption:
Freezing nights are on the way. Is your home policy ready for a burst pipe? 🧊

Most home policies treat water damage based on HOW it happened. A pipe that freezes and suddenly bursts is often considered sudden and accidental damage, which many policies cover. Water damage from a slow leak that went on for weeks, or from a pipe that froze because the home wasn't kept heated, is often treated as a maintenance issue and may be excluded.

A few simple habits help:
• Keep the heat at 55°F or higher, even when you travel
• Open cabinet doors under sinks on exterior walls
• Disconnect garden hoses and cover outdoor spigots
• Know where your main water shutoff is

Not sure how your policy handles water damage? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com for a free coverage review.

entries.title: A windstorm drops a tree on your car. Now what?
entries.caption:
Storm season in the Northwest means falling branches. If one lands on your parked car, which part of your auto policy steps in? 🌲

Damage from things like falling trees, hail, flooding, fire, theft and hitting an animal generally falls under COMPREHENSIVE coverage. Collision is for when your car hits another vehicle or an object, like a guardrail. And if you only carry liability coverage, damage to your own car usually isn't covered at all.

Comprehensive typically has its own deductible, so check what yours is before the next windstorm, not after.

Want a quick look at what your auto policy includes? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com.

entries.title: Forced out of your home? Who pays to live elsewhere
entries.caption:
If a fire or major water leak made your home unlivable tomorrow, where would you stay, and who would pay for it? 🏠

Many home policies include coverage often called additional living expenses, or loss of use. When a covered loss forces you out during repairs, it can help with the extra costs of living somewhere else, like a hotel or short-term rental, higher-than-usual food costs or extra mileage. It's generally meant to cover the increase above your normal expenses, not your regular bills.

This coverage usually has a dollar limit, a time limit or both, and it typically applies only when the damage itself is covered. Heating season and winter storms are a good time to know what yours looks like.

entries.title: Term vs. permanent life, in plain English
entries.caption:
Life insurance comes in two main families, and the names don't always make it obvious which is which. 💡

TERM life covers you for a set number of years, often 10, 20 or 30. If you pass away during that term, your beneficiaries receive the death benefit. It's built to protect people during the years they depend on you most, like while kids are young or a mortgage is being paid down.

PERMANENT life (such as whole life) is designed to last your whole life and typically builds cash value over time, which is one reason it generally costs more.

Neither one is "better." The right fit depends on how long you need coverage and what you want it to do. This post is educational only. Want to talk through which type fits your situation? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com.

entries.title: Comprehensive vs. Collision
entries.script: Last time, we decoded your liability limits. Today, let's settle the two coverages people mix up the most: comprehensive and collision. Collision covers damage to your car when it hits something, like another vehicle, a guardrail, or a pole. Comprehensive covers damage from almost everything else, like theft, hail, fire, falling trees, flooding, or hitting a deer. Both usually come with their own deductible, and both are about protecting your own car, not someone else's. If you only carry liability, neither one is on your policy, which means repairs to your car come out of your pocket. Here's your self-check. Look at your policy tonight. Do you see comprehensive and collision listed, and do you know each deductible? Next time, we'll tackle the phrase everyone uses but nobody defines: full coverage. Insurance in Laymens terms.

Comprehensive and collision sound alike but cover very different things. Here's which one steps in when, in plain English.

entries.title: Slid on ice into a guardrail? That's collision

Icy mornings are coming. If your car slides into a guardrail, a fence or another vehicle, here's how the coverage usually breaks down. ❄️

Damage to YOUR car from hitting something is typically handled by COLLISION coverage, after your deductible. Damage you cause to someone else's property, like their car or a guardrail, is generally handled by the property damage portion of your LIABILITY coverage. If you only carry liability, the repairs to your own car usually come out of your pocket.

Best protection is still prevention: slow down, leave extra space, and keep your tires in good shape.

Many home policies put a low limit on business equipment and inventory kept at home, and they often exclude liability that comes from business activities. So if a client trips on your front steps during a business visit, or your work laptop and inventory are stolen, your home policy might cover only a small part of it, or none at all.

entries.title: What an umbrella policy actually does
entries.caption:
An umbrella policy sounds fancy, but the idea is simple: it's extra liability protection that sits on top of your home and auto policies. ☂️

If you're found responsible for a serious accident or injury and the costs go past the liability limits on your home or auto policy, an umbrella policy can help pay the difference, up to its own limit. It can also cover some situations your other policies don't.

Umbrella coverage is worth a look if you own a home, have teen drivers, have a pool or trampoline, host often, or simply have savings and future earnings to protect.

entries.title: What "Full Coverage" Really Means
entries.script: Last time, we covered comprehensive and collision. Today, let's clear up a phrase you hear all the time: full coverage. Here's the surprise. Full coverage isn't an actual type of policy. Most people use it to mean liability plus comprehensive plus collision. But that combination can still leave gaps. It may not include things like rental car reimbursement, roadside assistance, or protection when the driver who hits you doesn't have enough insurance. And your limits matter just as much as the coverages themselves. Two people can both say they have full coverage and be protected very differently. So, self-check. If someone asked what's actually on your policy, could you list it? If not, that's a great reason to review it. Next time, we'll look at the coverage that protects you when the other driver can't pay. Insurance in Laymens terms.

• Towing to a repair shop
• Jump-starts for a dead battery
• Flat tire changes
• Lockouts and fuel delivery

It usually has limits, such as a maximum tow distance or a cap per service call, and it's typically only there if it was added to your policy. Cold snaps are hard on batteries, so now is a good time to check whether you have it.

If a tree falls on your house, garage or another covered structure, the damage to that structure is often covered under your home policy, and some policies also help with removing the tree. If the tree falls in the yard without damaging anything, removal often isn't covered, or is covered only up to a small limit. And if a tree was dead or decaying beforehand, coverage can get more complicated.

entries.title: Life insurance through work? Know the limits
entries.caption:
Have life insurance through work? It's a great benefit, but it may not be the whole picture. 💡

Many employers offer group life insurance, often a flat amount or a multiple of your salary. It can be a helpful starting point. A few things to know:
• It's often tied to your job, so it may end or change if you leave, retire or are laid off
• The amount may be less than your family would actually need
• You usually have less control over it than over a policy you own

An individual policy is one you own directly, so it generally stays with you no matter where you work. Many people use both together.

It's deer season on Northwest roads, and dusk comes early now. If one darts out in front of you, which part of your policy steps in? 🦌

Hitting an animal is usually handled under comprehensive coverage, not collision. That matters because the two often carry different deductibles, and comprehensive is optional, so it's only there if it's on your policy.

A few things to keep in mind:
• If you swerve to miss the deer and hit a guardrail or another car, that's often treated as a collision instead
• Liability-only policies generally don't cover damage to your own car either way
• Slowing down at dawn and dusk on wooded roads is still the best protection

entries.caption:
Quick question before the family gathers this week: do you know who's named as the beneficiary on your life insurance? 💡

The beneficiary is the person (or people) who would receive the policy's benefit. It's easy to set once and forget, but life changes. A marriage, divorce, new baby or a loss in the family are all good reasons to take a fresh look.

A few basics:
• A primary beneficiary is first in line; a contingent beneficiary is the backup
• Beneficiary designations are generally separate from your will, so updating one doesn't automatically update the other
• Group life through work has its own beneficiary form, too

Fire is generally one of the core perils a homeowners policy is built for. Depending on your policy, it can help with:
• Repairs to your home's structure (dwelling coverage)
• Damaged belongings, like furniture, dishes and small appliances (personal property)
• A place to stay if the kitchen is unusable (loss of use)

A few habits help keep the day on track: stay in the kitchen while frying or boiling, keep towels and packaging away from burners, and know where your extinguisher is. A lid slid over a small pan fire can smother it.

entries.title: How Usage-Based Insurance Works
entries.script: Last time, we covered protection from drivers who can't pay. Today, let's talk about usage-based insurance, sometimes called telematics. Here's how it works. With your permission, a phone app or a small device can track things like how hard you brake, how fast you accelerate, how often you drive late at night, and how many miles you drive. Depending on the program and your state, that information may be used to help set your rate. Safe habits can count in your favor, and some programs look at risky habits too, so know how a program works before you sign up. It's not right for everyone, and that's okay. Here's your self-check. Most homeowners and renters policies cover jewelry as personal property, but often with a special limit for theft. That limit can be much lower than the value of a nice piece.

An ice dam forms when snow melts higher on the roof, then refreezes at the colder edge. Water backs up behind the ice and can work its way under shingles and into ceilings and walls.

How a home policy may look at it:
• Sudden water damage inside your home is often covered, depending on your policy
• Long-term wear, maintenance issues or slow leaks usually aren't
• Removing the ice itself may not be covered

Clearing gutters, keeping snow off the roof edge when it's safe, and good attic insulation and ventilation can all help.

entries.title: Replacement Cost vs. Actual Cash Value
entries.script: Last time, we wrapped up our auto series. Now we're switching to home insurance, starting with two phrases that can change a claim check: replacement cost and actual cash value. Picture a kitchen fire that ruins a ten-year-old refrigerator. With actual cash value, the payment usually reflects what that fridge was worth after ten years of wear, which might not be much. With replacement cost, the payment is generally based on what it costs to buy a comparable new one today. The same idea can apply to your roof, your furniture and even the structure of your home, depending on your policy. Here's your self-check. Does your policy say replacement cost or actual cash value, and do you know which parts each one applies to? Next time, we'll look at dwelling versus personal property coverage. Insurance in Laymens terms.

entries.title: Gifts stolen from your car? Who covers what
entries.caption:
Holiday shopping means a trunk full of gifts. If someone breaks into your car and takes them, here's something that surprises a lot of people: your auto policy usually isn't what covers the gifts. 🎁

How it generally works:
• Damage to the car itself, like a broken window, is often handled under comprehensive coverage on your auto policy
• Personal belongings stolen from the car are usually covered under your homeowners or renters policy, depending on your policy and deductible

That means two different policies, and possibly two deductibles, can come into play.

A few habits help: keep gifts out of sight in the trunk, lock up every time and avoid leaving bags in the car overnight.

Questions about how your home and auto coverage work together? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com.

Coverage varies by policy, state and eligibility.

entries.title: Your home's market value isn't its rebuild cost
entries.caption:
Your home's market value and the cost to rebuild it are two different numbers, and your dwelling coverage is usually based on the second one. 🏠

Market value includes things like the land and your neighborhood. Rebuild cost is what it would take to repair or rebuild the structure itself, including labor and materials.

Why it matters:
• If your dwelling limit is lower than your rebuild cost, you could come up short after a major loss
• Construction costs can change over time
• Remodels, additions and upgrades can raise what it would cost to rebuild

The end of the year is a good time to check whether your dwelling coverage still fits your home.

entries.title: College kid home for break? Check their coverage
entries.caption:
Your college student is home for winter break, probably with a laptop and a car full of laundry. Is their stuff at school covered? 🎓

Depending on your policy, a homeowners policy may extend some coverage to a student's belongings while they're living away at school. A few things to know:
• That coverage is often limited, sometimes to a portion of your personal property limit
• It may depend on things like the student's age, enrollment and where they live
• Students living off campus in their own apartment may need their own renters policy

Break is a good time to check before they head back with new laptops and gifts.

Want to know how your policy handles a student away at school? Call (425) 419-0099 or email cody@lamensinsurance.com.
